title: Fastening off
subtitle: How to secure the last loop and close off a piece without leaving a weak point
excerpt: Fastening off is the few-second finish that stops a completed piece from unravelling. Done well it is invisible; done badly it pulls loose and undoes the work.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book. Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins).

glossaryTerms.definition: The loose end of yarn left after cutting at a fastened-off point or at a join. It is woven in to hide it and secure the end.
An adjustable loop that forms the starting point for the foundation chain. Pulling the tail tightens it; pulling the working yarn loosens it.

content.text: Fastening off is the way you secure the last loop on the hook after the final stitch of a piece or motif. Work it at the end of any section you are not continuing from: the last row of a flat piece, a completed motif, or a joined-in colour before switching to the next. The opening
tail from the foundation chain also needs securing when the piece is done; treat it the same as a fasten-off tail.
Work the final stitch of the piece to completion.
Cut the working yarn, leaving a tail of at least 15 cm. Longer is easier to weave in.
Draw the cut tail through the remaining loop on the hook and pull firmly. The loop closes to a small knot.
Thread the tail onto the tapestry needle and weave it into the fabric on the wrong side, working back and forth through several stitches to secure it.
Invisible fasten off for a seamless finish

The invisible fasten off hides the join point on the last round of in-the-round work. After the final stitch, cut the tail and draw it through the last loop as above. Then thread the tail onto the tapestry needle and insert it under both loops of the first stitch of the same round, pull through, then bring it back down through the centre of the last stitch. The tail forms a fake stitch that blends the join into the round.

on the wrong side of the work. Pass the needle through at least five or six stitches in one direction, then double back through a few in the opposite direction. This change of direction secures the tail against pull-out. Trim any remaining length close to the fabric.
Do not pull the tail too tight while weaving. Pulling gathers the fabric slightly on the right side.

items.symptom: The fastened-off tail keeps coming loose with use
items.cause: The tail was woven in only in a straight line with no change of direction, so tension on the fabric pulls it straight back out.
items.fix: Re-weave the tail. After going in one direction for five or six stitches, turn the needle and come back through two or three in the opposite direction before trimming.

items.symptom: The fasten-off point is visible on the right side as a small bump
items.cause: The last loop was pulled too tight, or the tail was trimmed too short and the knot sits on the surface.
items.fix: Leave the tail longer and weave it through one stitch before the knot to pull the knot to the inside of the fabric.

items.symptom: The slip knot at the start of the work comes undone when the tail is trimmed
items.cause: The starting tail was trimmed too short before it was woven in, leaving the initial knot without enough yarn to hold.
items.fix: Rethread the tail onto the tapestry needle and weave it back through at least five stitches before trimming. Leave 5 mm after the final weave before cutting.

content.text: Once standard fasten off is automatic, practise the invisible fasten off on a small granny square. The seamless join is worth learning early because it appears on almost every motif-based project.
